title: RBAC Model Reference (Console + API)
author: Ethan Park
body:
## Purpose
This page is the canonical reference for Redwood Inference’s role-based access control (RBAC) model used during enterprise security reviews. It covers:
- RBAC scope and objects (what can be controlled)
- Role definitions (Console + API)
- Permissions matrix (high-level, security-review-friendly)
- Least-privilege guidance and recommended setups
- Auditability notes (what events are logged and how reviewers can validate controls)

This page is written to be accurate across deployment modes (Hosted, Dedicated, Private) while clearly noting where capabilities vary.

## Scope and terminology
### Control plane objects
RBAC applies to actions in the Redwood control plane (Console and management APIs), including:
- Organization settings (SSO, domains, members, roles)
- Projects / workspaces (logical separation for teams/environments)
- API keys / service accounts (creation, rotation, revocation)
- Model access configuration (which models/routes a project can use)
- Usage and billing settings (invoices, usage export, budgets where enabled)
- Audit logging configuration and access (view/export depending on plan)

### Data plane actions (inference requests)
Inference requests are authorized via API keys (or service accounts) and are distinct from human user console access.
- A user’s Console role does not automatically grant data-plane inference access.
- Data-plane access is granted by issuing API keys/service accounts and scoping them to a project.

### Deployment mode notes
- Hosted / Dedicated: Redwood operates the control plane. RBAC, SSO, and audit logging are provided via Redwood Console.
- Private (VPC/on-prem): RBAC applies to the Private control plane instance. Some controls (e.g., log export integrations) may be customer-operated depending on architecture and contract.

## Identity sources and authentication
### Supported identity patterns
- Local (email + password) authentication may be enabled for smaller orgs and/or break-glass scenarios.
- Enterprise SSO (SAML) is supported for Console access.
- SCIM provisioning may be supported for automated user lifecycle management (create/deprovision, group mapping) when enabled.

See: security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth/sso-saml-and-scim-one-pager

### Recommended authentication posture (enterprise)
- Require SSO for all users (except controlled break-glass accounts).
- Enforce least-privilege roles per team function.
- Prefer SCIM for joiner/mover/leaver automation.
- Maintain a small number of Organization Owners (typically 1–2).

## RBAC model overview
RBAC is hierarchical:
- **Organization-level roles**: govern org-wide administration, identity, billing, and global settings.
- **Project-level roles**: govern project-scoped configuration, keys, and usage visibility.

A user may hold an organization role and one or more project roles. Effective permissions are the union of assigned roles.

## Role definitions
### Organization roles
1) **Organization Owner**
- Highest-privilege administrative role.
- Intended for a small set of trusted administrators.

2) **Organization Admin**
- Administrative role for day-to-day operations.
- Typically used by platform administrators / IT.

3) **Security Admin**
- Focused on identity, access, and audit posture.
- Does not manage billing (by default).

4) **Billing Admin**
- Billing and invoicing access; no security/identity administration.

5) **Org Read-Only (Viewer)**
- View-only access to organization metadata and dashboards.
- No ability to change configuration.

### Project roles
1) **Project Admin**
- Administer a project: members, API keys/service accounts, routing/config settings.

2) **Project Developer**
- Standard developer access: manage and rotate own project keys (where allowed), view project dashboards.

3) **Project Analyst (Read-Only)**
- View usage and operational dashboards.
- No ability to create/modify keys or configuration.

### Redwood internal access (Support)
Redwood employees are not granted access to a customer organization by default.
- Any support access to a customer tenant is controlled, time-bounded, and audited.
- For Private deployments, support access patterns are customer-configurable and depend on the deployment boundary.

## Permissions matrix (high-level)
Legend: ✅ Allowed | ⚠️ Allowed with constraints | ❌ Not allowed

### Organization-level permissions
| Capability | Org Owner | Org Admin | Security Admin | Billing Admin | Org Viewer |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| View org settings and members | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Invite/remove users | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Assign org roles | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ (cannot assign Owner unless Owner) | ❌ | ❌ |
| Configure SSO (SAML), domains | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Configure SCIM provisioning/mappings | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| Manage session/security settings (where available) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| View audit logs (org-wide) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ (view-only, if enabled) |
| Configure audit log export/integration (if enabled) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| View invoices, billing profile, tax/VAT | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ (read-only, if enabled) |
| Change plan/commit (contract-dependent) | ✅ | ⚠️ (may require Owner) | ❌ | ⚠️ (billing-only) | ❌ |

### Project-level permissions
| Capability | Project Admin | Project Developer | Project Analyst |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| View project settings | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Manage project members/roles | ✅ | ⚠️ (optional; commonly disabled) | ❌ |
| Create/rotate/revoke API keys/service accounts | ✅ | ⚠️ (own keys only; policy-dependent) | ❌ |
| View usage dashboards and request metrics | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| Configure routes/model access for project | ✅ | ⚠️ (optional; policy-dependent) | ❌ |
| View project audit events (project-scoped) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ (view-only) |

Notes:
- Some permissions are policy-dependent by plan, deployment mode, and/or feature flags (e.g., whether Project Developers can manage keys).
- Where both an org role and project role exist, the most permissive effective access applies.

## Least-privilege guidance (recommended setups)
### Recommended enterprise role assignments
- **Organization Owners (1–2 people):** IT/platform leadership or security leadership.
- **Security Admins (2–5 people):** security engineering, GRC (viewing/exporting audit events as needed), and designated admins for SSO/SCIM.
- **Billing Admins (1–3 people):** finance/RevOps.
- **Project Admins:** platform admins and a limited number of team leads.
- **Project Developers:** engineers who need operational visibility and routine key rotation.
- **Project Analysts:** stakeholders who only need reporting/visibility (security reviewers, compliance, leadership).

### Environment separation
Create separate projects for:
- Production
- Staging
- Development/sandbox

Benefits:
- Limits blast radius of keys and configuration.
- Enables narrower access grants (e.g., analysts can view prod usage but not modify prod keys).

### Key management and service accounts
- Prefer **service accounts** for automation/CI rather than personal user keys.
- Scope keys to the minimal set of projects and routes.
- Rotate keys on a defined cadence and immediately on suspected compromise.

### Break-glass access
For SSO-required orgs, maintain 1–2 break-glass accounts with:
- Strong authentication requirements
- Strict ownership and documented access procedure
- Routine access reviews

## Auditability and evidence notes
### What is audited
The audit log is intended to support enterprise-grade traceability for identity and administrative actions. Typical event categories include:
- Authentication and session events (e.g., SSO login success/failure, local login)
- User lifecycle events (invites, deprovisioning, role changes)
- SSO/SCIM configuration changes (IdP metadata, domain verification, SCIM token rotations)
- API key and service account lifecycle (create, rotate, revoke)
- Policy/config changes (project settings, route/model access changes where applicable)
- Administrative exports (e.g., audit log export job initiated)

See: security-and-compliance/audit-logging/audit-logging-overview-one-pager

### Event fields (typical)
Audit events generally include (exact fields may vary by event type):
- Timestamp (UTC)
- Actor (user/service account) and actor type
- Action/event name
- Target resource (org/project/key/user)
- Result (success/failure)
- Source context (e.g., IP address where captured, user agent where captured)

### How customers validate RBAC controls during review
Security reviewers commonly ask for:
- Evidence that only authorized roles can change SSO/SCIM settings
- Evidence of role changes and user deprovisioning
- Evidence of API key creation/rotation/revocation

Recommended validation steps:
1) Provide the RBAC matrix (this page) and the SSO/SCIM one-pager.
2) Provide sample audit events (redacted as appropriate) showing:
   - Role assignment change
   - API key rotation
   - SSO configuration update
3) Demonstrate in Console (live or screenshots) that a Viewer/Analyst cannot access admin controls.

### Access reviews
For enterprise accounts, recommend quarterly access reviews:
- Validate Organization Owner membership is minimal.
- Confirm Security Admin membership matches on-call/compliance needs.
- Confirm ex-employees are removed (SCIM deprovisioning logs can support this).

## Operational notes / common Q&A
### Can Redwood employees access our data?
RBAC described here controls customer-tenant access. Redwood internal access is governed by separate internal controls and is not “always on” to customer tenants. For Private deployments, the customer controls the deployment boundary and support access pattern; support access (if configured) should be time-bounded and auditable.

### Does RBAC restrict inference prompts/responses?
RBAC governs control plane actions. Data plane access is governed by API keys/service accounts and project scoping. Customers should:
- Separate prod vs non-prod projects
- Avoid sharing prod keys broadly
- Use service accounts and rotate keys

### Are there custom roles?
Custom roles may be available for select enterprise/private deployments but are not the default. If a prospect requires custom roles or fine-grained permissions beyond this matrix, route to Security & Compliance PM (Naomi Feldman) for scoping.

## Change management
- Changes to role definitions or permission boundaries must be reviewed by Security Engineering and GRC.
- Any customer-facing claims based on RBAC behavior should use approved language from the Security FAQ v2 and the Standard RFP Response Library.
